lines.text: Why did Anthropic stop using git, and what did they build instead?
In May, they merged 2,500 code changes a day.
With Claude, by September: over 30,000.
The bottleneck became tools built for humans, like git.
Git gives every copy the whole project and its entire history.
So you can work offline. For most projects, that's perfect.
But all of Anthropic's code lives in one giant project, with almost 100 gigabytes of history.
Each copy is over 25 gigabytes, and test jobs check out code 25 million times a day.
Hundreds of git mirrors and snapshots bought them time, but got harder to run as merges sped up.
Then they noticed: almost every user was an agent or an automated job, always online.
So why give each one a full copy?
So they built Scion, their own version control system.
The server holds the code and does the heavy work: history, commits, merges.
Each client keeps a small cache, a local copy of what it already fetched, and asks the server for the rest.
Every change is saved as a changeset: just the files that changed, with links to their contents.
Each link is made from the content itself, so the data never changes and any cache can keep it.
A client asks only for the folders it needs, starting from the top.
Some files arrive only when a program reads them.
When a job needs data, it looks nearest first.
First, scion-daemon: a cache on its own machine, shared by every job running there.
Next, scion-cache: servers in the same region that keep data ready in memory.
Last, the main scion servers: the source of truth, reading from the database and cloud storage.
Each layer answers over 99 percent of requests itself.
It needs 200 times less computing than their old git mirrors,
and checkouts take seconds, not minutes.
Many jobs never copy the code. They just ask the server, like: what changed in this commit?
Tools that find and undo bad changes work the same way.
With so many changes, making each one wait its turn doesn't work.
So changes land first, and tests run after.
If two clash, Claude usually fixes it before a human would notice.
The catch: a Scion client can't do much without the server.
Branches are discouraged, and code review, search and testing had to be rebuilt.
In return: far less data per copy, and a system that grows by adding machines.
So Anthropic says Scion isn't for most teams, only for giant codebases with swarms of agents.
Instead, they're sharing ideas that git could borrow.
Seven people built it in five months, with Claude.
Git copies everything. Scion asks only for what it needs. Follow for more AI basics.
